transcript.content: Hello. What brings you into the clinic today?

I keep forgetting my appointments and daily health stuff, even when I really try to stay on top of it. Ever since my heart scare last year, all these new doctor visits and pill schedules have just been piling up, and I'm really struggling to keep track of them.
Along with these memory struggles, have you been feeling persistently down, sad, or losing interest in activities you normally enjoy?

No, I haven't really been feeling down or losing interest in my activities at all. I still love going to the senior center and staying busy, but my main struggle is just keeping track of everything and managing these routines.
Apart from managing your appointments and medications, are you still able to handle daily tasks like dressing, bathing, and preparing meals completely on your own?

Oh, absolutely, I don't have any trouble with things like dressing, bathing, or cooking meals for myself. I can handle those basic daily tasks just fine on my own. My real struggle is just keeping track of all these doctor appointments and my daily medication schedule.
Are you still able to manage your appointments and medications on your own, perhaps by using notes or calendars, or do you now need someone else to handle these tasks for you?

I try using calendars and putting notes on the fridge, but I still get distracted and end up missing things completely. My nieces have actually started stepping in to help manage my pill boxes and online chart, which is frustrating because I really want to keep my independence.
Did you notice a sudden change in your memory and ability to keep track of things immediately after your heart scare, or has it been a gradual decline?

It wasn't a sudden memory loss or a gradual decline from the heart scare itself. Truth is, I've always been a bit disorganized and on-the-go, even going back to my school days. But that heart scare about 14 months ago dumped a whole load of new appointments and pills on me, which just completely overwhelmed my ability to keep track of things.
You mentioned being disorganized and on-the-go since school. Before the age of 12, did you have significant trouble with paying attention, sitting still, or finishing tasks at school or home?

Oh, absolutely, it goes way back. Even in grade school, my teachers were always sending notes home because I couldn't stay in my seat, talked over everyone, and kept roaming the classroom instead of doing quiet work. I was always getting in trouble for blurting things out instead of waiting my turn.
Nowadays, do you still find yourself feeling internally restless, having trouble sitting still, or frequently interrupting others and blurting things out?

Oh, definitely, it feels like I've got a motor running inside me that never shuts off, so I'm constantly bouncing my legs, shifting in my seat, or getting up to pace. And when my nieces try to help me with my medical charts, I find myself constantly jumping in, interrupting them, and finishing their sentences before they can even get a word out.

latest_inference.note: The patient reports a clear history of both inattentive and hyperactive-impulsive symptoms beginning in childhood (before age 12) and persisting into adulthood, causing significant impairment in managing her complex medical regimen and in her social interactions. This confirms a diagnosis of Attention-Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD), represented by ICD-10 codes F90.0 (Disturbance of activity and attention) and F90.9 (Hyperkinetic disorder, unspecified). No further questioning is required.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient meets the diagnostic criteria for Attention-Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ICD-10: F90.0, Disturbance of activity and attention). The patient exhibits a chronic, lifelong pattern of both inattention (forgetting appointments, difficulty managing medication schedules, being easily distracted and disorganized) and hyperactivity/impulsivity (feeling internally restless as if driven by a motor, constant pacing or shifting, interrupting others, and finishing sentences). These symptoms have been present since childhood (prior to age 12, as evidenced by school reports of being unable to stay seated, roaming the classroom, and blurting out answers) and currently cause significant functional impairment, requiring family members to step in and assist with daily instrumental activities.
